·

·

·

第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程

items.text:
Published Sep 13, 2026, 12:46 PM EDT

Arielle Port started as a TV producer, developing content for Netflix (Firefly Lane, Brazen) and Hallmark (The Santa Stakeout, A Christmas Treasure) before transitioning into entertainment journalism. Her love of story went from interest to lifelong passion while at The University of Pennsylvania, where she fell in with a student-run web series, Classless TV, and it was a gateway drug. Arielle Port has been a Writer for Screen Rant since August 2024. She lives in Los Angeles with her boyfriend and more importantly, her cat, Boseman.

Yellowjackets was originally conceived as a five-season story. The creators, Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson, have said they’ve learned valuable lessons from Lost about how to bring a long-running survival mystery series to a satisfying conclusion (via The Kingcast Podcast).

Like Lost, the first season of Yellowjackets walked a tightrope between the supernatural and the possibility that everything had a rational explanation. As the series has progressed, however, it has increasingly embraced its supernatural side, expanding its mythology while introducing even more unexplained phenomena and mysteries.

Season 2 often felt like it was stretching the story out, while Yellowjackets season 3 sometimes felt like it was racing to catch up. In 2025, Showtime and Paramount announced season 4 would be the final season of Yellowjackets, and the showrunners ultimately explained that the story made more sense as four tightly paced seasons than a meandering five.

Yellowjackets season 4, which premieres in November, will finally venture beyond the wilderness, exploring the rescue and the immediate aftermath of the girls' return to civilization. The season 4 trailer centers on the rescue, with the girls seemingly racing to bury their sins before it arrives.

In its final season, the wilderness-immersed teens will reenter society, while their middle-aged counterparts in the present grow ever closer to their wilderness selves. With so many mysteries still hanging over the survivors, season 4 has an enormous amount of ground to cover before the Yellowjackets’ story can finally land the plane.

The Wilderness Symbol

The Wilderness symbol has appeared throughout Yellowjackets since season 1, appearing everywhere from the tree near the crash site and the cabin attic floor to multiple trees in the wilderness. However, the series still hasn’t explained exactly what it means.

The mysterious symbol has inspired countless theories, with fans suggesting it could be a map, a hieroglyph, a ritualistic marking, or even a protection symbol. Its repeated appearances in different locations suggest it holds deeper significance beyond the cabin itself, but its origins remain unclear.

The symbol could also be connected to the mysterious individual who previously lived in the cabin and died there, potentially offering a clue about what happened before the Yellowjackets arrived. While the symbol may ultimately be connected to the Wilderness, its exact meaning, origin, and purpose remain some of the show's biggest unanswered questions.

The Power Of The Wilderness

Image via MovieStillsDB

Yellowjackets has done a brilliant job walking the line between the undeniably supernatural and the plausibly justifiable. At this point, it’s still debatable whether the Wilderness has any real power and, if so, how strong that power might be.

It’s equally possible that the Wilderness is simply a product of Lottie’s psychosis, the group’s drug-fueled hysteria, and their desperate desire to connect with something greater and find meaning in their tragedy. Some seemingly supernatural phenomena were explained rationally, like the mysterious screaming revealed to be frogs.

However, other events remain difficult to explain away, like Lottie's ability to walk unharmed over a pit, leaving open the possibility that something supernatural is at work. Before the series ends, Yellowjackets needs to finally reveal how much of the Wilderness is real and how much exists in the survivors’ minds.

The Hunter (AKA Cabin Daddy)

The show has referred to him more formally as the Hunter, but the fandom has settled on calling the body found on top of the Wilderness symbol in the attic in season 1 “Cabin Daddy.” The cabin man adds a Shining-like element to the cabin, suggesting that something disturbing may have happened there long before the Yellowjackets arrived.

The creators have confirmed that he matters to the larger story, rather than being nothing more than creepy set dressing. However, we still know almost nothing about his life or death.

Lottie might have channeled his spirit during a séance, telling the girls, “You must spill blood,” while Jackie might have seen him welcoming her in her final hallucination as she froze to death. He remains one of the show’s original mysteries, with surprisingly little of his story revealed.

Hannah’s Death

Image via MovieStillsDB

Hannah Finch is one of the scientists studying the Arctic Banshee Frog, and she deliberately ingratiates herself with the Yellowjackets. However, she isn’t simply pretending to assimilate. As Hannah becomes increasingly desperate to survive, she adopts the group’s worldview and commits increasingly horrific acts, including killing her former wilderness guide.

Yellowjackets season 3 established that Hannah is dead in the present timeline, while her recordings and records could become important evidence of what really happened in the wilderness. However, Yellowjackets has yet to reveal how or when Hannah died, making her fate one of the show’s newer mysteries.

The series has one season to explain Hannah’s ultimate fate. Hannah helped facilitate Natalie’s escape during the hunt in the season 3 finale, which is what will likely lead to the rescue. That also makes her an enemy to the newly crowned Antler Queen, Shauna, however.

The Cabin Fire

The season 2 finale deliberately made it seem like Coach Ben set the cabin on fire, but season 3 complicated that assumption without definitively clearing him. Many of the girls are convinced Ben was responsible, while Ben himself denies it.

There’s also something thematically strange about one of the few remaining symbols of civilization deliberately committing an act that could have killed the entire group. One of the most popular theories is that Other Tai started the fire, intentionally or accidentally; her sleepwalking has repeatedly connected her to unexplained events in the wilderness.

Yellowjackets has had three seasons that tell the stories of the plane crash survivors in the past and the present, but which season is the best?

Related

However, that remains only a theory, and Ben is still a possibility. Season 4 will have to finally reveal who or what started the fire and whether it was intentional.

Javi’s Friend

Image via MovieStillsDB

When Javi is found after surviving away from the group for months in season 2, he is nearly mute. One of the few things he says is that he found a friend in the wilderness who helped him survive, as he tells Coach Ben.

Ben later discovers the naturally heated cave where Javi had been living, but Javi's mysterious friend's identity remains unknown. It seems like a deliberately planted clue that could be important to the show's larger mythology, rather than something that can be dismissed as a hallucination.

If much of season 4 takes place after the Yellowjackets are rescued, however, there may be limited time to introduce a new character, whether Javi's friend is a real person or something more supernatural. If season 4 ventures back into the afterlife, Javi could finally answer the question.

Other Tai / Dark Tai

Image via MovieStillsDB

The show calls Tai’s subconscious form Other Tai, but the fandom has adopted Dark Tai. Dark Tai is clearly more than ordinary sleepwalking, as Other Tai can take control of her body, make decisions, travel, investigate, and act independently of Tai’s conscious awareness. This is especially clear when Other Tai breaks into Jessica Roberts’ apartment and later tracks down Van.

Season 3 also reveals the childhood ice-cream commercial that may have influenced Tai’s image of the Man With No Eyes, connecting it to her grandmother’s death. However, it’s still unclear how Other Tai can seemingly access information that conscious Tai doesn’t know, like what she actually wants, and how she is connected to the Wilderness.

The show has also hinted at a longer history of strange experiences in Tai’s family. Whether Dark Tai is rooted in trauma, psychology, something supernatural, or a combination of all three is still up for debate.

Walter’s True Motives

Walter, continuing Elijah Wood's streak of picking weird passion projects, seems to be Misty’s perfect counterpart. Like Misty, he is fascinated by true crime, possesses an unsettling willingness to cross moral boundaries, and seems to enjoy solving mysteries.

However, Walter also seems increasingly obsessed with the Yellowjackets, and it’s unclear whether he is fascinated by their infamous story, specifically obsessed with Misty, or pursuing some larger goal. He has investigated the survivors, helped Misty cover up Adam’s murder, and even killed Kevyn and framed him for Adam and Jessica’s deaths.

By the end of season 3, Walter is still keeping tabs on Misty and Tai, suggesting that his interest in the Yellowjackets is far from over. Fans have several theories concerning Walter's motivations, so season 4 needs to reveal exactly what he wants from the survivors and whether his fascination with them will ultimately help or hurt Misty.

The Plane Crash

The Yellowjackets were flying from New Jersey to Seattle for a soccer tournament when their plane went down in the Canadian wilderness. The plane encountered severe turbulence, and Laura Lee’s teddy bear burst into flames because of a mechanical issue.

However, the show has never definitively established that the crash was purely due to mechanical failure. Some have speculated that the Wilderness somehow caused or influenced the crash, or that Lottie’s father orchestrated it, though these are just theories.

There’s also the larger question of why this particular group ended up in this particular place. The crash feels potentially more significant than a random disaster. There’s also a practical mystery: why were the Yellowjackets trapped for 19 months?

Crystal’s Body

Image via MovieStillsDB

There are theories that Crystal survived the fall, but Misty, who is trained in CPR, saw and touched Crystal’s body while trying to revive her before the snow buried it. Crystal’s survival seems unlikely, but that still leaves one major question: what happened to Crystal's body?

After the storm, Misty specifically returns to find Crystal before the other girls can discover her, only to realize that the body is gone. Crystal is mentioned in passing in season 3, but the show still hasn’t explained where her body went or who, if anyone, found it.

Every season so far has had a surprise living Yellowjacket in the present timeline, making Crystal’s disappearance feel like too deliberate a loose end to ignore. Yellowjackets season 4 could finally reveal what happened to Crystal’s body, even if the answer confirms that she died in the wilderness.

blocks.x: The season 2 finale deliberately made it seem like Coach Ben set the cabin on fire, but season 3 complicated that assumption without definitively clearing him. Many of the girls are convinced Ben was responsible, while Ben himself denies it.

There’s also something thematically strange about one of the few remaining symbols of civilization deliberately committing an act that could have killed the entire group. One of the most popular theories is that Other Tai started the fire, intentionally or accidentally; her sleepwalking has repeatedly connected her to unexplained events in the wilderness.
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/every-season-of-yellowjackets-ranked.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=220&h=124&dpr=2
blocks.c: Custom image of Jackie (Ella Purnell) wearing a butterfly shirt and giving side eye and Lottie (Courtney Eaton) looking up with a smile in Yellowjackets

blocks.x: Yellowjackets has had three seasons that tell the stories of the plane crash survivors in the past and the present, but which season is the best?
Related
However, that remains only a theory, and Ben is still a possibility. Season 4 will have to finally reveal who or what started the fire and whether it was intentional.
Javi’s Friend
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/javi-yellowjackets.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Javi in the wilderness in Yellowjackets season 2

blocks.x: Image via MovieStillsDB

When Javi is found after surviving away from the group for months in season 2, he is nearly mute. One of the few things he says is that he found a friend in the wilderness who helped him survive, as he tells Coach Ben.

Ben later discovers the naturally heated cave where Javi had been living, but Javi's mysterious friend's identity remains unknown. It seems like a deliberately planted clue that could be important to the show's larger mythology, rather than something that can be dismissed as a hallucination.

If much of season 4 takes place after the Yellowjackets are rescued, however, there may be limited time to introduce a new character, whether Javi's friend is a real person or something more supernatural. If season 4 ventures back into the afterlife, Javi could finally answer the question.
Other Tai / Dark Tai
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tai-yellowjackets.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Tai and Other Tai have a conversation in the mirror in Yellowjackets

blocks.x: Image via MovieStillsDB

The show calls Tai’s subconscious form Other Tai, but the fandom has adopted Dark Tai. Dark Tai is clearly more than ordinary sleepwalking, as Other Tai can take control of her body, make decisions, travel, investigate, and act independently of Tai’s conscious awareness. This is especially clear when Other Tai breaks into Jessica Roberts’ apartment and later tracks down Van.

Season 3 also reveals the childhood ice-cream commercial that may have influenced Tai’s image of the Man With No Eyes, connecting it to her grandmother’s death. However, it’s still unclear how Other Tai can seemingly access information that conscious Tai doesn’t know, like what she actually wants, and how she is connected to the Wilderness.

The show has also hinted at a longer history of strange experiences in Tai’s family. Whether Dark Tai is rooted in trauma, psychology, something supernatural, or a combination of all three is still up for debate.
Walter’s True Motives
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/elijah-wood-s-walter-holding-his-hands-up-and-looking-bemused-in-yellowjackets.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Elijah Wood's Walter holding his hands up and looking bemused in Yellowjackets

blocks.x: https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/spectrum-on-demand-logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

Walter, continuing Elijah Wood's streak of picking weird passion projects, seems to be Misty’s perfect counterpart. Like Misty, he is fascinated by true crime, possesses an unsettling willingness to cross moral boundaries, and seems to enjoy solving mysteries.

However, Walter also seems increasingly obsessed with the Yellowjackets, and it’s unclear whether he is fascinated by their infamous story, specifically obsessed with Misty, or pursuing some larger goal. He has investigated the survivors, helped Misty cover up Adam’s murder, and even killed Kevyn and framed him for Adam and Jessica’s deaths.

By the end of season 3, Walter is still keeping tabs on Misty and Tai, suggesting that his interest in the Yellowjackets is far from over. Fans have several theories concerning Walter's motivations, so season 4 needs to reveal exactly what he wants from the survivors and whether his fascination with them will ultimately help or hurt Misty.
The Plane Crash
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/plane-crash-2.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: One Of The Soccer Girls Set On Fire From The Plane Crash In Yellowjackets Season 1, Episode 2, "F Sharp"

blocks.x: https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/image-3.png?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

The Yellowjackets were flying from New Jersey to Seattle for a soccer tournament when their plane went down in the Canadian wilderness. The plane encountered severe turbulence, and Laura Lee’s teddy bear burst into flames because of a mechanical issue.

However, the show has never definitively established that the crash was purely due to mechanical failure. Some have speculated that the Wilderness somehow caused or influenced the crash, or that Lottie’s father orchestrated it, though these are just theories.

There’s also the larger question of why this particular group ended up in this particular place. The crash feels potentially more significant than a random disaster. There’s also a practical mystery: why were the Yellowjackets trapped for 19 months?
Crystal’s Body
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/crystal-yellowjackets.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via MovieStillsDB

There are theories that Crystal survived the fall, but Misty, who is trained in CPR, saw and touched Crystal’s body while trying to revive her before the snow buried it. Crystal’s survival seems unlikely, but that still leaves one major question: what happened to Crystal's body?

After the storm, Misty specifically returns to find Crystal before the other girls can discover her, only to realize that the body is gone. Crystal is mentioned in passing in season 3, but the show still hasn’t explained where her body went or who, if anyone, found it.

Every season so far has had a surprise living Yellowjacket in the present timeline, making Crystal’s disappearance feel like too deliberate a loose end to ignore. Yellowjackets season 4 could finally reveal what happened to Crystal’s body, even if the answer confirms that she died in the wilderness.

items.title: Paramount files new legal statement saying states' antitrust suit misses the whole point of the merger
items.author: William Hughes

items.text:
Although they’re technically headed—due to a legally mandated step set forward by a judge—to the settlement negotiation table next month, Paramount and the coalition of state attorneys general currently trying to stand as the last roadblock in the company’s efforts to buy Warner Bros. moved past the point of civil conversation at least one “We’ll take the whole damn company out of Hollywood if you’re not careful” threat ago. As such, it’s not surprising that Paramount’s legal filings in the slowly brewing court case between the two are getting pretty belligerent, as the David Ellison-owned media company filed a new legal document on Friday that attempted a point-by-point dismantling of the states’ case. “Day by day,” the company’s lawyers write, “The weak case against this Merger gets even weaker.”


The gist of the argument, which was filed as a response to the AGs’ initial complaint, is one we’ve seen from Paramount before, back when it was getting bogged down in arguments about whether Curry Barker’s indie horror hit Obsession counts as a “blockbuster”: That the states’ case against the merger is built off of an older understanding of Hollywood that sees major studios like Paramount and Warner Bros. as main, direct rivals for each other—which ignores, they argue, the reality of tech-derived companies like Netflix, Apple, and Amazon breaking into the market over the course of the 21st century. In what, to the best of our knowledge, is the only legal filing between a large Hollywood studios and 12 American states to acknowledge the existence of that upcoming Netflix theatrical movie where Taika Waititi plays an ex-con Willy Wonka, the response argues that the streamers are already stomping all over the theatrical market, and that the only way for old Hollywood (as represented by David Ellison, a guy who’s owned a major studio for all of two years because his tech billionaire dad gave him some pocket change) to fight back is to merge into a cinematic kaiju of its own. (The Godzilla metaphor is our own, sadly, and not part of the legal filing.)


There are other aspects to the response, with Paramount making the requisite attacks on the states’ ability to litigate an antitrust issue that’s already been cheerfully cleared by Ellison’s buddies in the Department Of Justice. (With the paragraph-by-paragraph addressing of each of the original complaint’s points including such lawyers-are-certainly-human-beings-type language as “Defendants admit that the State of Oregon is a state of the United States.”) Among other things, the filing points to the fact that all three of America’s major theater chains have stated that they want the merger, apparently convinced of Ellison’s claims that ParaBros. (or whatever they end up calling this new city-stomping behemoth) will keep big movies rolling out at a steady pace. (The assertion that Cinema United, the trade organization representing the chains, is calling for a settlement in the case does blithely paper over the fact that the group has not actually gone so far as to endorse the plan, though.)


There will, of course, be more of these backs-and-forths as the negotiations approach and then, it seems very probable, recede. (Both sides are reportedly pretty intransigent in their belief in the merits of their arguments; also, given the politicized overtones of all this, we’d be shocked if any of these AGs blinked before the elections in November.) The most interesting aspect of the whole thing, meanwhile, might come down to a point not articulated in Paramount’s new filing at all: Whether (per Variety) Paramount will get its demand that the states pony up a bond covering the costs of delaying the merger, estimated at nearly $2 billion thanks to the “ticking fee” Paramount agreed to give Warner Bros. if the sale got delayed. Even split across 12 states, that’s a lot of cash, with Paramount clearly attempting to extract some real blood in exchange for the AGs attempts to get in the way of its big kaiju dreams.

items.text:
Tom Hardy's Hit Crime Series Officially Gets Its Season 2 Debut This Week

Image via Famous/ACE PICTURES/INSTARimages.com

Guy Ritchie's Netflix series The Gentlemen returned with a second season earlier this month, although viewership was down by around 45% in its first week. It is believed that the longer shows take between seasons, the higher the chances are of fans dropping out. The Gentlemen took around two years to return, but Ritchie's other hit show has a better chance of succeeding purely because it's coming back within a year of its premiere. The show in question made a splashy debut on Paramount+ in 2025, breaking viewership benchmarks set by Taylor Sheridan's platform-defining hit Yellowstone. Awareness for the series didn't dip even during the off-season, thanks to the many controversies that it found itself embroiled in.

It was reported that star Tom Hardy had been fired from the project's future seasons after he had a run-in with some key creatives. This was later revealed to be false, but not until several reports had emerged claiming to detail what went down. Hardy's feud with Charlize Theron on the set of Mad Max: Fury Road was cited as proof of his on-set behavior, but it was eventually revealed that not only had Hardy not been fired, but he would be returning to headline the show in a confirmed third season. All of this is to say that Paramount+ is highly bullish about the series, which follows the Godfather template but unfolds in contemporary London.

Collider Exclusive · Taylor Sheridan Universe Quiz
Which Taylor Sheridan
Show Do You Belong In?
Yellowstone · Landman · Tulsa King · Mayor of Kingstown

Four worlds. All of them brutal, complicated, and built on power, loyalty, and the price of survival. Taylor Sheridan doesn't write heroes — he writes people who do what they have to do and live with the cost. Ten questions will reveal which one of his worlds you were made for.

🤠Yellowstone

🛢️Landman

👑Tulsa King

⚖️Mayor of Kingstown

FIND YOUR WORLD →

01

Where does your power come from?
In Sheridan's world, everyone has leverage. The question is what kind.

ALand, legacy, and a name that's been feared and respected for generations.
BKnowing the deal better than anyone else in the room — and being willing to walk away first.
CReputation. I've earned it the hard way, and everyone in the room knows it.
DBeing the only person both sides will talk to. That makes me indispensable — and dangerous.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Who do you put first, no matter what?
Loyalty in Sheridan's universe is always absolute — and always costly.

AFamily — blood or chosen. The ranch, the name, the people who carry it with me.
BThe company — or whoever's signing the cheques. Loyalty follows the contract.
CMy crew. The men who stood with me when it counted — I don't abandon them for anything.
DMy community — even when my community is a powder keg and I'm the only thing stopping it from blowing.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Someone crosses a line. How do you respond?
Every Sheridan protagonist has a line. What matters is what happens after it's crossed.

AQuietly, decisively, and in a way that sends a message to everyone watching.
BI outmanoeuvre them legally, financially, and politically before they even know I've moved.
CDirectly. Old school. You cross me, you hear about it to your face — and then you deal with the consequences.
DI absorb it, calculate the fallout, and find the move that keeps the whole system from collapsing.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

Where do you feel most in your element?
Sheridan's worlds are as much about place as they are about people.

AWide open land — mountains, sky, silence. Somewhere you can see trouble coming from a mile away.
BThe oil fields of West Texas — brutal, lucrative, and indifferent to whoever happens to be standing on top of them.
CA mid-size city where the rules haven't quite caught up yet — fertile ground for someone with vision and nerve.
DA rust-belt town built around a prison — where everyone's life is shaped by what's inside those walls.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How do you feel about operating in the grey?
Nobody in a Sheridan show has clean hands. The question is how they carry the dirt.

AI do what has to be done to protect what's mine. I'll answer for it eventually — but not today.
BGrey is just business. The line moves depending on what's at stake, and I move with it.
CI have a code — it's not the law's code, but it's mine, and I don't break it.
DI've made peace with it. Keeping the peace requires compromises most people don't have the stomach for.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

What are you actually fighting to hold onto?
Every Sheridan character is fighting a war. The real question is what they're defending.

AA way of life that the modern world is doing everything it can to erase.
BMy position — and the leverage that comes with being the person everyone needs to close a deal.
CRelevance. I've been away, I've been written off — and I'm proving that was a mistake.
DWhatever fragile order I've managed to build — because without it, everything burns.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

How do you lead?
Authority in Sheridan's world is never given — it's established, maintained, and constantly tested.

ABy example and force of will. People follow me because they believe in what I'm protecting — and because they know what happens if they don't.
BThrough negotiation and leverage. I don't need people to like me — I need them to need me.
CBy being the smartest, most experienced person in the room and making sure everyone quietly knows it.
DBy being the calm centre of a situation that would spiral without me — and accepting that nobody thanks you for it.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

Someone new arrives and tries to change how things work. Your reaction?
Every Sheridan show has an outsider disrupting an established order. Sometimes that outsider is you.

AThey'll learn. Or they won't. Either way, the land was here before them and it'll be here after.
BI figure out what they want, what they're worth, and whether they're an asset or a problem — fast.
CI was the outsider once. I give them a chance — one — to show they understand respect.
DNew players destabilise everything I've built. I assess the threat and manage it before it manages me.

NEXT QUESTION →

09

What has your position cost you?
Nobody gets to where these characters are without paying for it. The bill is always personal.

AMy family's peace — maybe their innocence. The ranch demands everything, and I've let it take too much.
BRelationships, time, any version of a normal life. The job eats everything that isn't nailed down.
CYears. Decades in some cases. Time I can't get back — but I'm not done yet.
DMy conscience, mostly. And the ability to ever fully trust anyone on either side of the wall.

NEXT QUESTION →

10

When it's over, what do you want people to say?
Sheridan's characters all know the ending is coming. The question is what they leave behind.

AThat I held the line. That the land is still ours and everything I did was worth it.
BThat I was the best at what I did and that no deal ever got closed without me at the table.
CThat I built something real, somewhere nobody expected it, and I did it on my own terms.
DThat I kept the peace when nobody else could — and that the town is still standing because of it.

REVEAL MY SHOW →

Sheridan Has Spoken
You Belong In…

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

🤠
Yellowstone

🛢️
Landman

👑
Tulsa King

⚖️
Mayor of Kingstown

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

items.title: A24 somehow making an SCP movie without anybody from The SCP Foundation involved
items.author: William Hughes
items.summary: The SCP Foundation is one of the most fascinating collaborative projects in internet history: An effort, touched by thousands of hands over nearly two decades,
items.text:
The SCP Foundation is one of the most fascinating collaborative projects in internet history: An effort, touched by thousands of hands over nearly two decades, to create a shared horror universe based around a mysterious organization and its attempts to create “special containment protocols” for objects of anomalous, and frequently apocalyptic, power. Featuring horror, fantasy, science fiction, comedy, and an absolutely huge amount of black redacting bars, the site has been running for 16 years at this point, and has been the basis for any number of video games, podcasts, and online shorts. So while it was probably inevitable that Hollywood would eventually start sniffing around the project, it is a bit surprising to learn that A24 is moving forward with plans for an SCP film without anyone involved in the creation of The SCP Foundation being involved.


The studio’s involvement broke online on Friday, via a report from Deadline stating that A24 had come aboard a previously mentioned effort to adapt the SCP setting into the existing V/H/S/ horror franchise. The article noted that Image Nation Studios and Spooky Pictures were involved in the film’s production; what it didn’t mention, beyond a claim to “worldwide rights” to the project, was which members of the guiding group for The SCP Foundation Wiki might be involved.


None, apparently: In a statement to The A.V. Club, The SCP Foundation Wiki Licensing Team wrote that, although members of the team have attempted to reach out to the filmmakers about the project, “We have not had any communication with the filmmakers, producers, or distributors for this project, despite our best efforts, and to the best of our knowledge they have not made any efforts to contact us.” They also called Deadline‘s claim of “worldwide rights” “incorrect,” citing the terms of the Creative Commons ShareAlike license the entire Wiki is released under.


Ownership is the big, flashing question mark hanging over all of Hollywood’s recent efforts to shove online horror into a theater-shaped box. On the one end, you have projects like Zach Cregger and Brian Duffield’s recently announced Siren Head movie, where the duo are working from clearly copyrighted materials licensed from artist Trevor Henderson. On the other, there’s A24’s own Backrooms, which, while based on director Kane Parsons’ YouTube-published short films, was clearly beholden to the communal setting Parsons was inspired by. The SCP wiki sits in a unique position between those two extremes: The Licensing Team’s statement noted that, while many derivative works have been made using the SCP name, all such projects are required to also carry the CC BY-SA license that the entire archive, and the idea of SCPs themselves, exists under. Among other things, honoring that license means A24’s movie would need to be released without “DRM or other effective technological measures that would prevent it from being copied,” and, probably most crucially, “They would not be able to establish any sort of exclusivity with respect to distribution”—meaning the film would be freely available to upload to YouTube, or even commercial streaming platforms, without the studio being able to say a word.


Which doesn’t seem like something A24 would just put up with—something the Licensing Team’s statement notes is a major reason Hollywood has never bit on SCP before, despite its online popularity. (While also making it wild that the filmmakers would specifically use the group’s name, instead of trying to fudge around it.) We’ve reached out to A24 to try to get a response to the Foundation’s assertion of the terms of its license; so, for that matter, has the Licensing Team, which had the following to say in conclusion:


We’d love to sit down with A24, Spooky Pictures, and other involved parties to discuss options for how they could make and distribute a film while complying with our license. We chose to release our project under a Creative Commons license to allow fans to tell their own stories as well as adapt ours. We chose the ShareAlike license to ensure that everyone who enjoyed those fan works would have the same rights as the people who created them. We’re getting frustrated with this whole situation and are disappointed that these filmmakers seem to have no interest in engaging with the authors or curators of the material they’re adapting.

items.title: Wardogs presents a different kind of FPS power fantasy: making fat stacks as a pacifist rideshare driver
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer
items.text:
Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer shooter in which I’ve just found employment. Its "Play like to you used to" tagline and Halo 3-aping trailer smell a bit of reactionary, stuck-in-the-past thinking. It’s a mass-scale multiplayer shooter, so individual heroics rarely influence match outcomes. And, like pretty much everyone else who sucked down both those problems and tried playing on launch night regardless, I spent far too long attempting to communicate with server architecture that clearly had the resilience of overmilked cornflakes.

And yet, the fifty minutes I did spend in a functioning match felt like some of the most pleasant and productive time I’ve had in a competitive FPS for ages. The secret: ignore all first person shooting entirely, and begin a lucrative career as an Uber driver for commuting mercs.

In a stark break from reality, Wardogs’ gig economy can be very profitable indeed. Almost every positive action earns you cash, from the obvious hardpoint captures and squadmate revives to the humble delivery of people and bandages to the frontlines. And, since team spawns are literal miles from the central battlezones, logistical roles are not merely cash-incentivised, but essential.

In an accurate reflection of reality, you begin with little, must buy all vehicles and equipment yourself, and are on the hook if they’re lost while on duty. But the creation of genuine rear-detachment roles means Wardogs solves problems I have with both big shooters, and the extraction subgenre it also borrows from: by constantly ferrying teammates, I can have an individual yet materially important impact on the match, and by never intentionally joining a gunfight, I need never worry about loot loss anxiety. It was the perfect career move.

Buoyed by first-day enthusiasm, once I finally loaded into a game I bought a car, directed it dutifully towards the crowd of pedestrian soldiers, and immediately caused a helicopter crash. My pull-up-to-the-kerb manoeuvre had unwittingly put me in the landing path of a descending attack chopper – a major fault in the standard United Kingdom driving test – forcing the delicate warbird to flip over my roof and explode. Its occupants, miraculously unhurt but quite cross, shot me a damning glance as they strode off to buy another one.

The rest of my inaugural fare, a full house of one real-life friend and two silent randomers, went mercifully smoother. Despite the slippery handling of my entry-level SUV, it was a comfortable, peaceful drive towards the hot zone, which itself offered ample parking space for my passengers to hop out. The prizes came instantly: $1,000 for a "tactical deployment", plus $500 for each of my unharmed passengers, plus a $15 tip from a particularly satisfied rider. $2,515 for a few kilometres of relaxed cruising? The hell am I doing as a deputy ed?

The private hire lifestyle took hold. For multiple runs, I’d steer back to base, wait next to other transit vehicles (sometimes sharing an “A’ight, mate” with the heli pilot next to me), load up on balaclava men, and deliver them vaguely near the sound of gunfire, my balance swelling with each trip. Half an hour in, I’d accumulated slightly higher earnings than my IRL friend, who’d been running around murdering people and getting shot himself. Sounds painful. Sounds like participating directly in the horrors of war, mankind’s most terrible creation, and a blight on the Earth that continues to destroy families and erase cultures every day. Sounds like he’s not even getting paid that much to do it anyway, the rube.

Meanwhile, my hands were clean, not counting all the filthy lucre that was crossing it. Granted, my usefulness was starting and ending with the thunk of automobile doors – sometimes I’d watch my disembarked comrades perish just moments after paying their fare, a tragically premature "Passenger survived, +$500" lingering onscreen as their heaped form shrunk in my rearview. In these moments I was less Iqbal, the friendly Prius owner who got me home from the pub last week, and more Charon, damned soul ferryman of the River Styx.

As the match went on, I also began having trouble with that key component of hypercapitalism: competition. It turned out those heli pilots were not my mates at all, but were conspiring to steal my business, adopting the unfair and likely illegal practice of having faster vehicles than me. Eventually, my stream of human tip jars reduced to a trickle of stragglers, the larger crowds routinely making a beeline for the nimbler, more spectacular choppers.

In search of alternative revenue streams, I diversified into supply logistics. At this point I hadn’t made quite enough profit to afford a proper truck, so instead bought one empty crate, chucked a few cheap medical supplies into it, and bunged it my car's back seat. Seemingly in ignorance of the massive boot, but whatever. I knew delivering it somewhere useful would require driving deeper into the fray than my people-carrying had thus far, but shareholder value (mine) demanded it.

The journey was, again, uneventful, and I chanced upon a makeshift base swarming with more action-inclined teammates. Surely, the kind of folk who’d appreciate a box of plasters. Not entirely familiar with the controls, I hit the G key to unload, at which point the create seemed to disappear. A "Supplies delivered, +$500" popped up – which, as my accountant tells me, if half what I could have made by filling those seats with bums instead – but I remained concerned about the supplies themselves. Beginning my search, I reversed, directly onto and over the bandage box that has been laying just out of view. Now, I was stuck, the car’s back end suspended barely high enough for the rear-wheel-drive wheels to regain purchase on the tarmac.

This was not ideal. As I got back at the wheel and tried wriggling free with Game Physics sorcery, I noticed the allies I’d come to resupply were no longer dashing around on the roof. Within seconds, a lone, green-dressed man with no 'Don’t shoot this one' arrow above his head rounded the building’s corner, rifle raised. Still stuck, I killed the engine and did the best impression of an empty, slightly slanted car that I’ll ever have to do. The man’s scope swivelled in my direction, then kept going, the ruse successful long enough for an arrowed teammate to pop out from behind a van and shoot him down.

Hands sweating in gratitude, I eventually managed to slide my bumper free and roar off back to HQ, alive and enriched. My shift was only brought to an end by a return of those blasted server errors, but I clocked off a happy man: I’d nearly tripled my net worth and had been, more so than in any Battlefield game I’ve ever bumbled through, helpful. Honestly, what a silly slogan – why play like you used to when you can start an exciting new career in personal transportation?

And, like pretty much everyone else who sucked down both those problems and tried playing on launch night regardless, I spent far too long attempting to communicate with server architecture that clearly had the resilience of overmilked cornflakes.

And yet, the fifty minutes I did spend in a functioning match felt like some of the most pleasant and productive time I’ve had in a competitive FPS for ages. The secret: ignore all first person shooting entirely, and begin a lucrative career as an Uber driver for commuting mercs.

In a stark break from reality, Wardogs’ gig economy can be very profitable indeed. Almost every positive action earns you cash, from the obvious hardpoint captures and squadmate revives to the humble delivery of people and bandages to the frontlines. And, since team spawns are literal miles from the central battlezones, logistical roles are not merely cash-incentivised, but essential.

In an accurate reflection of reality, you begin with little, must buy all vehicles and equipment yourself, and are on the hook if they’re lost while on duty. But the creation of genuine rear-detachment roles means Wardogs solves problems I have with both big shooters, and the extraction subgenre it also borrows from: by constantly ferrying teammates, I can have an individual yet materially important impact on the match, and by never intentionally joining a gunfight, I need never worry about loot loss anxiety. It was the perfect career move.

Buoyed by first-day enthusiasm, once I finally loaded into a game I bought a car, directed it dutifully towards the crowd of pedestrian soldiers, and immediately caused a helicopter crash. My pull-up-to-the-kerb manoeuvre had unwittingly put me in the landing path of a descending attack chopper – a major fault in the standard United Kingdom driving test – forcing the delicate warbird to flip over my roof and explode. Its occupants, miraculously unhurt but quite cross, shot me a damning glance as they strode off to buy another one.

The rest of my inaugural fare, a full house of one real-life friend and two silent randomers, went mercifully smoother. Despite the slippery handling of my entry-level SUV, it was a comfortable, peaceful drive towards the hot zone, which itself offered ample parking space for my passengers to hop out. The prizes came instantly: $1,000 for a "tactical deployment", plus $500 for each of my unharmed passengers, plus a $15 tip from a particularly satisfied rider. $2,515 for a few kilometres of relaxed cruising? The hell am I doing as a deputy ed?

The private hire lifestyle took hold. For multiple runs, I’d steer back to base, wait next to other transit vehicles (sometimes sharing an “A’ight, mate” with the heli pilot next to me), load up on balaclava men, and deliver them vaguely near the sound of gunfire, my balance swelling with each trip. Half an hour in, I’d accumulated slightly higher earnings than my IRL friend, who’d been running around murdering people and getting shot himself. Sounds painful. Sounds like participating directly in the horrors of war, mankind’s most terrible creation, and a blight on the Earth that continues to destroy families and erase cultures every day. Sounds like he’s not even getting paid that much to do it anyway, the rube.

Meanwhile, my hands were clean, not counting all the filthy lucre that was crossing it. Granted, my usefulness was starting and ending with the thunk of automobile doors – sometimes I’d watch my disembarked comrades perish just moments after paying their fare, a tragically premature "Passenger survived, +$500" lingering onscreen as their heaped form shrunk in my rearview. In these moments I was less Iqbal, the friendly Prius owner who got me home from the pub last week, and more Charon, damned soul ferryman of the River Styx.

As the match went on, I also began having trouble with that key component of hypercapitalism: competition. It turned out those heli pilots were not my mates at all, but were conspiring to steal my business, adopting the unfair and likely illegal practice of having faster vehicles than me. Eventually, my stream of human tip jars reduced to a trickle of stragglers, the larger crowds routinely making a beeline for the nimbler, more spectacular choppers.

In search of alternative revenue streams, I diversified into supply logistics. At this point I hadn’t made quite enough profit to afford a proper truck, so instead bought one empty crate, chucked a few cheap medical supplies into it, and bunged it my car's back seat. Seemingly in ignorance of the massive boot, but whatever. I knew delivering it somewhere useful would require driving deeper into the fray than my people-carrying had thus far, but shareholder value (mine) demanded it.

The journey was, again, uneventful, and I chanced upon a makeshift base swarming with more action-inclined teammates. Surely, the kind of folk who’d appreciate a box of plasters. Not entirely familiar with the controls, I hit the G key to unload, at which point the create seemed to disappear. A "Supplies delivered, +$500" popped up – which, as my accountant tells me, if half what I could have made by filling those seats with bums instead – but I remained concerned about the supplies themselves. Beginning my search, I reversed, directly onto and over the bandage box that has been laying just out of view. Now, I was stuck, the car’s back end suspended barely high enough for the rear-wheel-drive wheels to regain purchase on the tarmac.

This was not ideal. As I got back at the wheel and tried wriggling free with Game Physics sorcery, I noticed the allies I’d come to resupply were no longer dashing around on the roof. Within seconds, a lone, green-dressed man with no 'Don’t shoot this one' arrow above his head rounded the building’s corner, rifle raised. Still stuck, I killed the engine and did the best impression of an empty, slightly slanted car that I’ll ever have to do. The man’s scope swivelled in my direction, then kept going, the ruse successful long enough for an arrowed teammate to pop out from behind a van and shoot him down.

Hands sweating in gratitude, I eventually managed to slide my bumper free and roar off back to HQ, alive and enriched. My shift was only brought to an end by a return of those blasted server errors, but I clocked off a happy man: I’d nearly tripled my net worth and had been, more so than in any Battlefield game I’ve ever bumbled through, helpful. Honestly, what a silly slogan – why play like you used to when you can start an exciting new career in personal transportation?

items.title: Stylised XCOM-like tactics game Ex Sanguis straps Othercide's obsession with timelines to a leaner roguelike campaign
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: The nasal greenhorn strategy gamer understands "strategy" to be about mastery of space by means of clanging offensives, shining shieldwalls, and brute
items.text:
The nasal greenhorn strategy gamer understands "strategy" to be about mastery of space by means of clanging offensives, shining shieldwalls, and brute attrition, but the true Napoleon of Drag-Select knows that strategy is always, primarily, the mastery of time. I don't think Napoleon would have approved of Ex Sanguis. He would not have liked all the willowy clone women made out of congealed blood and pincers. He would have suspected them of being divorcees and Babouvists. But perhaps he would have appreciated the game's fixation with seizing the initiative.

As with Lightbulb's previous grid-based tactics RPG Othercide, Ex Sanguis has you going up against dozens of vaguely eschatological bladespawn with just the three austere and menacing bladegirls. There are generally a half-dozen foes to start with, and reinforcements soon hatch from gross eggsacs around the map. You can't simply overwhelm your opponents, then. Instead, you must pre-empt and interrupt them, anticipating their advance and dancing your best moves in first on the game's fluctuating timeline.

Some abilities are performed instantly, while others trigger after a delay. However initially inconvenient, the delays soon become an asset, as you learn to aim your artillery strikes where you know your enemies will be, a few score ticks from now. Other abilities trigger when an opponent acts, cutting them off. Or when a friendly deals some damage, adding a follow-up attack. A key question is whether to exhaust your regular action points and dip into your Burst bar, which lets you sneak in some extra licks at the cost of wildly postponing the character's next turn.

Watch on YouTube

And then there's repositioning: you get shoves, gravity pulses, and driving kicks that punt opponents around. This allows you to knock delayed enemy attacks off target, perhaps slamming the noxious seraphim into a boulder, or nudging them into the path of the AOE move you've just queued up with the previous character. As you preview these gambits, the character portraits and action indicators shuffle to and fro on the timeline. On higher difficulties, it's vitally important to avoid a scenario where the whole opposing force can take a turn, one after the other.

When I played Othercide, I didn't quite clock how much Lightbulb's approach has in common with Into The Breach. The resemblance feels a bit more prominent in Ex Sanguis. There's no fixed match countdown, true, but you're encouraged to finish fast: the angelbeasts are only going to get more numerous, and you generally aren't required to slaughter all of them - just a surgeon's handful of VIPs or a single enemy map fixture, sulking to the rear.

It's a messier experience than you'll find in Subset's game, however. The environments are full of blood blisters that blow up when struck, launching nearby characters a few squares. On more crowded maps, a single volatile pustule often triggers a prolonged cascade. The AI in the early access build seems overfond of setting the blisters off, in addition to controlling terrain. Some times, it's hellbent on swarming you; at others, it tries to lock down big portions of the map by preparing a delayed AOE move, wherever it finds itself.

The greater emphasis on terrain damage is one thing that distinguishes the early access version of Ex Sanguis from what I remember of Othercide. The other, more obvious point of departure is that Ex Sanguis has a trimmer roguelike structure, with more focussed progression.

On which note, here's my best effort at explaining the story: some kind of pesky vampire moon has leeched away the world's vital fluids and memories, reducing all of Creation to an ivory placeholder. You are the Mater, a goddess replete with the simmering intensity of Derek Zoolander. She can spawn duplicates of herself to fight the moon's minions. So far, it's very much the previous game's gothic mommy monster mash on fast-forward – all pout and glare and cod Latin metaphors, without much coherence but with a lot of enjoyable attitude.

It feels faster partly because there's less going on outside battle. Each run kicks you off with three warriors, allowing you to pick their classes – the initial options are broadly Swordlady, Gunlass and Time Wizardress - and starting abilities. You then trek across a cratered world map, fighting battles (with unlockable higher difficulties) and accumulating Corrupted Blood for campaign progression. Every battle you win nets you a choice of three further abilities or stat boosts per character.

Yes, we are operating in the realm of Vampire Survivors, just a teeny bit. As in the previous game and many other roguelikes, abilities form complementary sets, which are fun to unearth: for example, Swordlady can inflict bleed with one kind of melee attack, then slurp up the debuff to restore her own health. Eventually, you swill down enough Corrupted Blood from victories to access a bossfight, which functions as a chapter break. It's wise, of course, to pootle around a bit first, levelling up your murderdames and spending a bit of your Corrupted Blood on smaller lore discoveries that come with bonus abilities. When a run is over, whether due to beating a boss or defeat, you'll spend various flavours of ethereal substance on meta-unlocks that give you more things to unlock within runs.

I'm mixed on the new campaign format. I do miss the grottier, denser storytelling of the previous game, which grounded its stark monochrome abstractions in a narrative of obscure medieval abuses: it was like a neo-noir penny dreadful. I also took ghoulish pleasure in the ability to melt down your clone-daughters into primordial soup, treating the weaker ones as health packs for their more accomplished sisters, rather than just levelling everybody up. It's possible there are similarly revolting ideas at play later in Ex Sanguis.

Beyond that, I do wonder how much the new game's battle system and ability design really improves on Othercide's. I haven't yet discovered a blend of reaction and delayed abilities that really captivates me, in terms of how it lets me mess with the timeline and disrupt the horde.

Still, it's early days – I've only played three hours, and Ex Sanguis will spend at least six months in early access. If you really loved Othercide, I don't think there's anything here that will hugely disappoint you, just yet. You can read more about the game on Steam. Belated clarification: you do not have to be Napoleon or any other celebrated general to have opinions about Ex Sanguis. I'm not sure how Napoleon found his way into my intro, honestly.

items.title: Skyrim’s official IKEA crossover mod might be the most deftly-assembled Elder Scrolls gag ever, if not an ad blueprint other corps should follow
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim
items.text:
I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim as an official Bethesda-approved Creation, that I’d now be sitting here noting that I dug said creation’s dungeon designs.

I am, though, because I think that sums up the entire experience of playing through Kallax Storageborn. If all you do is read a headline about it or scan through the premise with a smirk, you might assume it’s just a soulless corporate stunt aiming to play off The Elder Scrolls 5’s well-established viral memeality, but without any depth that makes it worth dedicating the time to check out. That was largely how I felt about it too, up until I learned that highly skilled Fallout 4 Sim Settlements makers Kinggath Creations were the modders behind the free creation, and decided to check their work out for myself.

The secondary motivation I had for doing so was that in-game advertising feels like it’s being floated more often than ever at the moment as a way games might help pay for themselves, as the squeeze is felt across an industry desperate for maximum financial returns. Fantasy RPGs like Skyrim are arguably among the toughest places to naturally fit such ads, especially compared to the likes of sports games or James Bond adventures with special watches.

In terms of how it fits in Tamriel, you’ll probably be glad to learn that outside of loosely meshing with Skyrim’s established mechanics, Kallax Storageborn isn’t trying too hard to pretend that its additions are in any way lore-friendly. The first time you’re overencumbered after grabbing the mod, your character is sent a magical talking telegram informing them that a solution to their storage woes can be found in a dungeon called Storereach. Yep, that’s the tone set then.

Storereach starts off as a regular Skyrim cave, but grows into a well-made Dwarven dungeon assembled mostly from recognisable vanilla building blocks. Things really kick into gear when you reach the second level, Storereach Workshop. Here, the standard swells of Skyrim’s orchestral soundtrack morph into the quiet, but unmistakable jingle of distant elevator music as you wander into a Dwarven department store. In case you’re unsure, an apparition materialises to welcome you. If you’re anything like me, you’re completely distracted by the fact that next to him are specially made Dwarven versions of IKEA’s flatbed shopping trollies.

From there, you negotiate a maze of dioramas showing off Dwarven furnishings for different rooms, some of which have buttons you can press to trigger a short demonstration by ghostly salespeople. You learn about Stenrygg seats, Tavan rugs, and Gruskok kitchen sets. The place isn’t just an empty show hall, though: there’s some unique gear and a couple of secrets that are easily missed if you don’t peek around as many corners as you might in a standard dungeon delve. While some of the gags - such as a shield with a deflection enchantment dubbed the ‘Shield of the Returns Policy’ - are rather groan-worthy, a couple properly tickled me. For instance, I stumbled across a skeleton in the loos, bearing a note indicating they’d died after simply getting lost among the labyrinthine halls of the shop. That’s the sort of joke people make about going to IKEA, rather than one the retailers themselves would necessarily make, since it suggests their signage is a bit crap. It’s the sort of touch that stops the creation feeling too reverent or robotic in its efforts to convince you to buy a flat-pack bookcase called Billy, even when it’s giving you a spell that fires the retailer’s famous Swedish meatballs.

The mod’s main draw and namesake awaits in a chamber behind the store. Armed with a tome perfectly mimicking an IKEA instruction manual, and a staff shaped like an allen key, you assemble Kallax. Once its shelves have been inserted, this unit springs to life and starts speaking in comedian Matt Berry’s dulcet tones. He’s a new follower who’ll scrape along the ground behind you as you adventure and carry all of your burdens, much like a certain base game lady whose name rhymes with an STD. Cool. This is about where I expected the adventure to end, once I’d taken one more wander around Storereach to make sure I’d maxed out a loot haul that’s very potent if you rock up at a low level fresh out of Helgen. I can confirm that because I had to start over to try the IKEA mod, as a result of still not having gotten around to making sure my mod load order’s been updated to match last month’s new patch.

Alas, my adventure with Kallax was only beginning. After I’d crafted him his own version of Skyrim’s iconic iron helmet, he had me off to two more dungeons in search first of heirlooms from his missing master, and then in search of an assistant who might be able to shed light on his reason for existence. Along the way, I grew to love not so much Berry’s array of unique lines responding to places I visited and hijinks I got up to, but the more subtly hilarious touch of his footsteps constantly resembling the low rumble of wooden furniture being dragged along stone roads and through grassy undergrowth.

Eventually, we cornered the assistant in an ancient Nordic ruin chock full of clutter that you can order Kallax to clean up in order to unblock passages. I won’t spoil the ending, but I will note that the final chamber’s utterly majestic, and that along the way you’ll encounter the last few long-running Skyrim jokes the mod’s yet to hit. Many who’re sick of such gags and have low tolerance for any form of advertising will understandably roll their eyes so many times they end up unable to stop looking at the inside of their own heads.

I found it creative, well-crafted, and self-aware enough not to grate on me. I’m not even much of a Matt Berry fan either, which I think speaks to the job Kinggath and co have done of taking what could have been a licence to phone it in and trying just as hard as they would with a non-ad project. Even if they did miss out one key item from their Dwemer emporium. Without having to lean on the mad Daedric prince Sheogorath - the ever-present crutch of any Elder Scrolls wackiness which threatens to tap on the fourth wall - they’ve created an officially rubber-stamped gag that’s worth more than five minutes of a player’s time.

That said, I don’t think Kallax Storageborn should necessarily serve as an example any corps or developers should look at when trying to insert their own palatable ads into Skyrim or any other game. The line it walks between endearing - if nakedly corporate - charm and off-putting cringe is very thin, and successfully negotiating it relies heavily on the unique blend of British and Scandinavian humour at play. If it were, say, an advert for a more American brand like Monster Energy or Little Caesars, I think it’d feel a lot more in-your-face and forced. Due to its meme-filled reputation, in large part built on the back of unofficial joke mods, Skyrim also suits this sort of tongue-in-cheek salespersonship a lot more easily than other RPGs. It’s an exception to the rule, rather than an ideal test case.

So, leave the neatly stored memories of captivating, if not overly lengthy, dungeons alone please. This shelving unit came together well, but it shouldn’t inspire legions to believe they can assemble an entire floor’s worth of bookcases without ending up with at least one screw out of place.

Without having to lean on the mad Daedric prince Sheogorath - the ever-present crutch of any Elder Scrolls wackiness which threatens to tap on the fourth wall - they’ve created an officially rubber-stamped gag that’s worth more than five minutes of a player’s time.

That said, I don’t think Kallax Storageborn should necessarily serve as an example any corps or developers should look at when trying to insert their own palatable ads into Skyrim or any other game. The line it walks between endearing - if nakedly corporate - charm and off-putting cringe is very thin, and successfully negotiating it relies heavily on the unique blend of British and Scandinavian humour at play. If it were, say, an advert for a more American brand like Monster Energy or Little Caesars, I think it’d feel a lot more in-your-face and forced. Due to its meme-filled reputation, in large part built on the back of unofficial joke mods, Skyrim also suits this sort of tongue-in-cheek salespersonship a lot more easily than other RPGs. It’s an exception to the rule, rather than an ideal test case.

So, leave the neatly stored memories of captivating, if not overly lengthy, dungeons alone please. This shelving unit came together well, but it shouldn’t inspire legions to believe they can assemble an entire floor’s worth of bookcases without ending up with at least one screw out of place.

items.title: “Marvel’s Wolverine” is a Bloody Good Time, Bub
items.author: Brian Tallerico
items.summary: Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s
items.text:
Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s long-awaited release of Insomniac’s “Marvel’s Wolverine,” a game with structural echoes of the company’s beloved “Spider-Man” games, with significantly less kid-friendly violence and more linear, intense storytelling. After a prologue/tutorial that feels a bit rocky in storytelling and gameplay, “Wolverine” settles in spectacularly, strapping players into a rollercoaster narrative and telling them not to panic. With remarkably fluid combat, gorgeous graphics, strong voice work, and compelling storytelling, this is one of the best games of 2026, which has already been a remarkably great year for gaming before roughly a dozen more intriguing titles come out before Thanksgiving. The Sony disc drama aside, it’s a good time to be a gamer.

“Marvel’s Wolverine” also owes a wonderful amount to the movies most readers have probably seen about the man with Adamantium bones. At first, it feels like it’s intentionally echoing the excellent “Logan,” the best film about this beloved character, in its sketch of a slightly older Wolverine forced into a protective role for more vulnerable mutants when the evil Bolivar Trask starts kidnapping them. The plan to eradicate mutantkind sends Logan back to his allies at Team X, including founder Nathaniel Essex and familiar faces like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Jean Grey, sketched very differently here than the Sadie Sink version from “BND.” More on that later.

After Team X rescues a group of mutants from Trask’s captivity, including Callisto, “Marvel’s Wolverine” pivots again to incorporate other comic book and film source material. It’s the kind of story that never directly mimics something you’ve seen before, but one can definitely feel the influence of Bryan Singer’s films on Logan’s search for identity and even Jean Grey’s ultimate arc (don’t worry, comic fans—I didn’t just spoil that it goes full Dark Phoenix à la the horrendous “The Last Stand”). As the story moves to Japan, it also brings in some of that country’s influence on this character, as seen cinematically in James Mangold’s underrated “The Wolverine.” You’ll even get to slice and dice your way through hundreds of members of The Hand, also seen in the best action sequence in “Brand New Day.”

And I do mean slice and dice. Parents should be warned that this game is far more violent than they may expect from the developers of “Miles Morales.” The developers don’t dull Logan’s blades in the slightest, allowing you to use them to stab, mutilate, and decapitate on a regular basis. The combat gameplay is familiar in its mix of strike, parry, dodge, and special powers, but it’s as fluid as any game like this that’s ever been released. As techniques, unlike new skills that recharge over time and one improves at the base mechanics, Wolverine becomes almost a Tasmanian Devil of a killing machine, taking enemies out at a rate befitting one of comicdom’s most beloved heroes. It gets to the point where one sees a dozen enemies and doesn’t question how to get through them but wonders why there aren’t more. By the time I got into my New Game Plus playthrough, I had fully mastered the combat of “Wolverine” as much as any game in years, and the adrenaline rush of a perfectly executed move simply never abates. I’ll honestly miss it.

Of course, a game can’t just be about decapitating fools who underestimated a man with claws. As for the rest of the experience, the set pieces are so spectacular that you can forgive the lackluster exploration. As for the latter, Logan often has to find something in a room to push the story forward, which basically just amounts to looking for the white dot that cues you to hit triangle. It’s not exactly thrilling. On the other hand, there are a couple of motorcycle set pieces that are so spectacular that you’ll wish there were more of them, and the big action sequences are as impressive as any MCU movie. The truth is that “Marvel’s Wolverine” gets the big and basic things right; so the minor connective tissue like running around the Team X facility to find the triangle that will push the story forward isn’t really a drag as much as a little break from the intensity before it becomes numbing.

Something else that elevates “Marvel’s Wolverine” over many games of this generation is its attention to environment. As you can imagine, when Logan turns into a blade whirlwind, nothing is safe, and the designers brilliantly allow you to leave a mark, whether it’s just a blade scratch on metal or something more intense. For example, you get into a fight in an arcade in Japan, and no claw machine is safe. Most combat sequences end in the kind of environmental destruction rarely seen in games where you can still take cover behind a wooden box, and it’s the kind of detail that really elevates the overall experience. It should also be noted that this game makes use of the PS5 controller in expansive ways, whether it’s a radio signal or just the hum and buzz of action. And the load times are insanely fast. You can go from startup to combat in actual seconds.

Finally, while “Marvel’s Wolverine” is incredibly fun, it’s also narratively richer than many superhero games. Without spoiling, Logan and Jean Grey become allies not just in stopping the big bad of this game but in figuring out the details of Logan’s lost past. Like in the Singer movies and some of the comic arcs, Logan is a killing machine who doesn’t really know how he got that way, and the script here lands in a place that’s both satisfying and poignant. It’s as rich as the great Uncanny X-Men arcs that this comic book fan grew up loving, and a reminder of how both superhero fiction and gaming can be so much more satisfying when it’s developed with true love, care, and mutilations.

Sony provided a review copy of this game. It is available on September 15, exclusively on PlayStation.
