items.title: Bargain with demons and boat with the dead in joyful RPG heist quest anthology Thousand Hells
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the
items.text:
You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the designers of King of Dragon Pass is an absolute tonic. It's a witty procession of Orphic descents, in which you assemble a crew of four garrulous weirdos and pitch them against quest scenarios that might involve talking trees, holy riddlers, and conduits of boiling blood.

There's an infectious, venturesome lightness to the game, which somehow persists alongside dire blunders and supernatural calamities that may see members of your party being cursed, punctured or unhinged. I've only completed a couple of the 10 heists across two hours of play, which makes me reluctant to call this an official review, but it's got my provisional recommendation. Come, reader - get thee to Pandemonium apace.

Watch on YouTube

Thousand Hells doesn't harbour a thousand distinct hells; its variety comes, instead, from choice of party members and the canny reshuffling of story beats, which play out against handsome paintings of monoliths, bazaars, shorelines and catacombs. Each run starts with your character accepting One Last Job from some dubious power-broker in the "Byzantine-flavored" Eternal City. Perhaps you'll be looking into the untimely deaths of some princelings, or maybe you'll be escorting a murderer: either way, you'll need to trek down to an underworld that borrows ideas from Ancient Greece and Mesopotamia.

The opening interview also defines your character, as you pick from backgrounds, strengths and faults. Ho thar! I am Caroline, seasoned sailor and scout, with the bestest biceps this side of the Hungry Sea. My major shortcoming: I like to make jokes about gods.

Having created yourself, you then recruit a crew of similarly imperfect adventurers, spending Question points to decide how much you know about them to begin with. A big hand for Sethre: diplomat, pickpocket and shaman, dream-dogged and impulsive. A round of applause for Hemze: catfooted spymaster, who looks like a bull's derriere. The characters you choose will form loose relationships, reacting to each other's traits as the yarn wears on. These relationships are strongly shaped by the task at hand, which might see you keeping secrets from your colleagues, or deciding in advance that somebody ain't coming back from the Great Below.

The heist itself consists of a series of round-based encounters drawn from a pack of over 280, each with a mix of solutions depending on your party's skillset. In a pleasing tactile device that makes me think yet again of Ursula K Le Guin, encounters are resolved using bags of tokens. Each round, you pull up to four tokens from three bags. You get one bag for the character you've selected to take charge of the encounter (which means you'll be able to play more of their tokens), and one for the rest of the group. A third bag houses tide-turning boons and knowledge you may have acquired by, say, befriending a sorrowful spirit, or jailbreaking a god.

The tokens mostly reflect each character's traits, both helpful and hindersome – "Nerinai is knowledgeable", "Chisu is greedy", "Sethre has a troubled past", "Esanth knows lockpicking". You apply these tokens to one of three actions, corresponding to the scenario. You're navigating the rapids of Styx: do you focus on the rocks, or on the unruly dead crowding the stern? You're helping the Fates weave your very own destiny: do you throw the shuttle, or offer to cut the warp threads?

Other, more generic tokens might grant you resources and buffs, or rid you of debuffs. Show Some Swagger will improve a character's morale, if played successfully, while Get The Measure earns you Insight points, which let you visualise the odds of each token being successful. Any tokens and actions not used up in a round carry over to the next, so you might want to reserve any tokens that could fit several possible actions. Conversely, you'll need to figure out when to dispose of tokens that seem bound to fail. "Hemze is ugly" probably does have a use at some stage – I dunno, maybe Narcissus is working a guard post somewhere, and you can invite him to give Hemze a makeover? - but I'm not sure it's going to help me rescue some drowning merchants.

You need to win a certain number of rounds, and avoid a certain number of losses, but fumbling the encounter doesn't end the game: you might incur an injury or receive a mood penalty, perhaps even lose a character, but you'll often achieve the story objective (like crossing a river) regardless. I've rarely felt the urge to reload a save, which isn't possible anyway.

While never a taut exercise in resource juggling, the encounter design does oblige a bit of strategy, thanks to some underlying combos and questions of timing. Some actions are best performed early, boosting your chances of doing something else – disarming traps before lunging for a treasure, for instance. Some are easier to do when you're ahead or behind on victory points. A few need to be reserved for the encounter's finale.

Sometimes you get a bunch of tokens that don't entirely fit any action, and must guess how the writers will play out the implications. So far, I've found those stabs in the dark more entertaining than jarring, but there have been a couple of moments when the storycraft felt somewhat meaningless, next to the invisible tallying of points. Over the course of the heist, you also need to think about gathering items that serve as quickfix solutions, sometimes allowing you to avoid an encounter.

As you'd expect from the whole "repeatedly going to hell" premise, the encounters can be pretty macabre. During my first run, I had to deal with some hags who can shave away character traits with a nasty look. During my second, I tackled a scenario for which a positive outcome would see a character being hung from a meathook.

There are plague crows, blade tsunamis, and mesmerising demons. Worst of all, there's a poetry contest. (I won the poetry contest, mostly by alternating between mockery of my opponent and flattery of the audience.) As grim as things may get, however, the writing remains brisk and buoyant, with characters squabbling a bit and maybe revealing something about themselves when they strike out, keeping up the momentum of the tale. I've come to love these little setbacks. It's like Scheherazade turning every tumble into a cliffhanger, with her head on the line. It's the kind of game in which a clean sweep feels like a loss, because you've bleached away the reversals and pratfalls that any thrilling adventure should involve.

Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists is out now on Steam. I reckon you should give 'er a go, especially if you enjoyed the art and writing of King of Dragon Pass and its spiritual successor, Six Ages, but found the village management element tedious. I should mention that the game's writers include Holly Nielsen, who has done stuff for RPS in the past.

items.title: TIFF 2026: 20 World Premieres We Can’t Wait to See This Year
items.author: Brian Tallerico
items.summary: It’s that time of year again! We’re back with a big team at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, which starts tomorrow with one of the biggest
items.text:
It’s that time of year again! We’re back with a big team at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, which starts tomorrow with one of the biggest programs in the festival’s history. Like every other year, TIFF is a mix of North American, International, Canadian, and World Premieres. It will give many people their first chance to see films from Cannes like “Fjord” and “Clarissa,” along with several Venice and Telluride options like “Wild Horse Nine” and “Ink.” While we plan to hit several films in Canada that other outlets have covered from Venice and Telluride (including highly anticipated titles like “Elsinore” and “Possible Love”), we always focus our annual preview on 20 movies playing nowhere but TIFF.

Come back for coverage of all 20 of these, plus about two dozen more, from yours truly, Marya E. Gates, Cortlyn Kelly, and Zachary Lee.

Note: All of the synopses below are from the official TIFF site.

“Babies”

Anchored by a pair of hugely appealing lead performances from Seth Rogen (TIFF ’25’s Good Fortune) and Oscar nominee Anna Kendrick (TIFF ’09’s Up In the Air), the second feature from writer-director Lauren Miller Rogen (Like Father) digs deep into the dilemma that comes for every couple: to parent or not to parent? Bolstered by an all-star ensemble that includes Issa Rae (TIFF ’23’s American Fiction), Dan Stevens (TIFF ’25’s Swiped), and Oscar nominees Sharon Stone (Casino) and David Strathairn (Good Night, and Good Luck), Babies is relatable, hilarious, and wise in equal measure.

“Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo”

A dizzyingly prolific auteur who never fails to imprint his signature on every project he undertakes, Japanese maestro Takashi Miike (TIFF ’01’s Ichi the Killer) returns to the Festival with this thrilling contribution to a one-of-a-kind cinema legacy. Like Abel Ferrara’s cult masterpiece Bad Lieutenant (TIFF ’92) and Werner Herzog’s gonzo Southern neo-noir Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call — New Orleans (TIFF ’09), Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is very much its own entity, not so much a sequel to its predecessors as a mood, a variation on shared themes, and a rollercoaster ride through the darkest crevasses of the Tokyo underworld.

“Being Heumann”

Every bit as moving as her Best Picture Oscar winner, CODA, Siân Heder’s Being Heumann tells the remarkable true story of the woman who led a world-changing campaign for accessibility. Judy Heumann rallied a handful, then dozens, then hundreds of ordinary Americans with disabilities to push the US government to live up to its commitments.

The year is 1977. Raised in Brooklyn by German Jewish immigrants, and using a wheelchair since a childhood case of polio, Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) knows it takes grit and tenacity to get things done. So when Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo) refuses to sign meaningful regulations for Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the first national civil rights legislation designed to provide protections for people with disabilities, Judy devises a plan to force his hand, beginning with the occupation of a federal building in San Francisco, before going all the way to DC — and Califano’s front door — with a diverse team of self-described “radical crips,” creating solidarity through coalitions of marginalized groups.

“Closing Night”

Actor Cody Fern (American Horror Story, The Great Darkened Days, TIFF ’18) makes a sensational directorial debut with this sharp, emotionally astute story about family bonds and buried truths. When an internationally renowned movie star (Sarah Paulson) invites her estranged family to the opening night of her Broadway play after decades of silence, old wounds resurface almost as quickly as old habits. Her emotionally fragile sister (Naomi Watts, The Friend, TIFF ’24) remains determined to hold onto a lifetime of resentment, while her nephew (Toby Wallace, Finestkind, TIFF ’23) sees an opportunity to forge a relationship with his famous aunt.

“Diary of a Mad Old Man”

This captivating chamber drama from versatile auteur Wayne Wang (last at the Festival with 2019’s Coming Home Again) draws us into the troubled psyche of an aging widower whose sudden onset of disability coincides with the development of an unnervingly intimate relationship. Featuring a brilliantly graded performance by veteran actor Lily Franky (familiar to TIFF audiences from Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Shoplifters and Chie Hayakawa’s Renoir), this adaptation of revered Japanese author Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s eponymous novel ushers us into a realm of beguiling signals and unruly desire.

“Everybody Wants to F*ck Me”

Taron Egerton gives a gleefully committed performance as Adam in Jonathan Schey’s darkly comedic debut, riffing on the dating scene and the self-proclaimed “nice guys” who litter it. Adam has mastered all the trappings of enlightened masculinity: listening more than speaking in meetings with women coworkers, reading feminist literature, practicing yoga, and offering a soupçon of self-deprecation when chatting up women at bars or on dating apps. Adam’s longtime friend who once provided cover for his behaviour is growing up and growing weary of being an accomplice.

Adam has had a lifetime of f*ck around, but his find out is just around the corner when he meets Jessica Henwick’s Sofia. Intriguing and sharp, she proves to be a challenge calling out his behaviour. We’re back with a big team at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, which starts tomorrow with one of the biggest programs in the festival’s history. A Finnish Metal Detectorist Was Shocked to Unearth a Trove of Viking Age Silver in His Hometown. Then His Detector Went Off Again

Weighing a combined ten pounds, the artifacts are estimated to be 1,000 years old and constitute Finland’s largest coin hoard of the era

A metal detectorist in southern Finland has unearthed the country’s largest hoard of Late Iron Age silver coins to date. Buried in the 11th century in what’s now the town of Sysmä, the ten-pound collection contains remnants of jewelry and likely thousands of coins.

The detectorist, Kalle Lappinen, was scanning ground in his hometown last week when his metal detector signaled. He began digging, and then his handheld probe “roared,” Lappinen tells the New York Times’ Ephrat Livni.

“With the fury of a monkey, I dug through the soil, bottom moraine and cobblestones,” he recalls. He found “a pile of coins” about 18 inches down and, once he had “recovered from the adrenaline rush,” reported it to authorities. Then, not far away, Lappinen’s metal detector signaled again, prompting him to dig a second hole—and find yet another trove of coins.

Did you know? The Staffordshire Hoard

One of the most famous discoveries by a metal detectorist was made in 2009, when Terry Herbert unearthed an astonishing

cache of some 3,500 pieces of early medieval gold and silver metalwork in Staffordshire, England, that were eventually valued at more than $5 million.

The next day, Esko Tikkala, an archaeologist at the nearby Lahti City Museums, arrived to inspect and excavate the artifacts. According to a statement from the museums, the collection includes a fragment of hacksilver, a silver bracelet, a silver charm, a silver bead and many silver coins—which have not yet been cleaned, separated or counted. The coins alone weigh just under ten pounds; experts say there must be thousands.

“There are quite a lot of coins in this hoard,” and they await detailed analysis, Tikkala tells Live Science’s Tom Metcalfe. “There will definitely be scientific articles published on the hoard as a whole, as well as more detailed studies of the coins themselves.”

The hoard likely dates to between about 1000 and 1050 C.E., Tikkala says. This half-century corresponds with the tail end of the Viking Age, which historians typically confine to about 793 C.E.—when Vikings raided Lindisfarne in Britain—through 1066, the date of the Norman Conquest. Lahti City Museums have thus classified the hoard as a “Viking Age” find.

“The term ‘Viking Age’ does not imply that there were Vikings in Finland,” Tikkala explains. “We have no sources suggesting that Finland was ‘Viking’ in the same sense as regions of present-day Sweden, Norway and Denmark.”

Though Finland isn’t Scandinavian and wasn’t Viking territory, by the 11th century, some Swedes had settled on its southern coasts. As Toni Paukku, an archaeologist at the Lahti Museums, tells the Times, “Finland was strongly connected to the Scandinavian cultural sphere, boosted by the trade of Scandinavian seafarers—some of whom were indeed Vikings—across the Baltic Sea.”

The silver hoard found by Lappinen was buried in two birch-bark containers, about 40 feet apart, per the statement. Experts don’t know why it was buried, but historians do know that the close of the Viking Age was an unstable period in Finland, as Swedes and Danes raided its regions where Finns, Russians and Germans traded.

“Intentionally hidden treasures like these are somewhat common for this era in Finland,” Paukku tells the Times, citing societal unrest due to external threats. “One can only say that whoever they”—the people who hid the silver—“were, they did not come back to collect the treasure. … No burials appear to be associated with the hoard.”

Lappinen’s find marks the latest in a remarkable tally of silver discoveries this year. Just over a week ago, a Dane landscaping in his backyard accidentally unearthed Denmark’s largest hoard of Viking silver, and in April, metal detectorists in Norway found their country’s largest deposit of Viking silver. The Sysmä collection has easily taken the title of Finland’s largest silver coin hoard, which previously belonged to a five-pound stash unearthed near the southern coast in 1895.

The Sysmä discovery is “a case of responsible and responsive detecting, which has produced a promising archaeological discovery,” Eljas Oksanen, an archaeologist at the University of Helsinki, tells the Times. It shows that “detectorists can produce a considerable amount of new valuable information about the past, not the least because they (as in this case) search in areas that professional archaeologists do not go to.”

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/8gdXaSlownm90ER2-4v_Hvhd-_Q=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1477x1392:1478x1393)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/41/b6/41b67ab1-77ef-49b6-b5e7-2a61fb295d4e/viikinkiaikainen_rahakatko_1.jpeg

The hoard likely dates to between about 1000 and 1050 C.E., Tikkala says. This half-century corresponds with the tail end of the Viking Age, which historians typically confine to about 793 C.E.—when Vikings raided Lindisfarne in Britain—through 1066, the date of the Norman Conquest. Lahti City Museums have thus classified the hoard as a “Viking Age” find.

“The term ‘Viking Age’ does not imply that there were Vikings in Finland,” Tikkala explains. “We have no sources suggesting that Finland was ‘Viking’ in the same sense as regions of present-day Sweden, Norway and Denmark.”

Though Finland isn’t Scandinavian and wasn’t Viking territory, by the 11th century, some Swedes had settled on its southern coasts. As Toni Paukku, an archaeologist at the Lahti Museums, tells the Times, “Finland was strongly connected to the Scandinavian cultural sphere, boosted by the trade of Scandinavian seafarers—some of whom were indeed Vikings—across the Baltic Sea.”

The silver hoard found by Lappinen was buried in two birch-bark containers, about 40 feet apart, per the statement. Experts don’t know why it was buried, but historians do know that the close of the Viking Age was an unstable period in Finland, as Swedes and Danes raided its regions where Finns, Russians and Germans traded.

“Intentionally hidden treasures like these are somewhat common for this era in Finland,” Paukku tells the Times, citing societal unrest due to external threats. “One can only say that whoever they”—the people who hid the silver—“were, they did not come back to collect the treasure. … No burials appear to be associated with the hoard.”

Lappinen’s find marks the latest in a remarkable tally of silver discoveries this year. Just over a week ago, a Dane landscaping in his backyard accidentally unearthed Denmark’s largest hoard of Viking silver, and in April, metal detectorists in Norway found their country’s largest deposit of Viking silver. The Sysmä collection has easily taken the title of Finland’s largest silver coin hoard, which previously belonged to a five-pound stash unearthed near the southern coast in 1895.

The Sysmä discovery is “a case of responsible and responsive detecting, which has produced a promising archaeological discovery,” Eljas Oksanen, an archaeologist at the University of Helsinki, tells the Times. It shows that “detectorists can produce a considerable amount of new valuable information about the past, not the least because they (as in this case) search in areas that professional archaeologists do not go to.”

items.text:
Did You Suffer a Sweltering August? You Weren’t Alone. It Tied for the Month With the Hottest Global Temperatures on Record

Last month, the air temperature averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit, tying with July 2023 as the toastiest month ever documented by the European Union’s climate service

Sara Hashemi
| Daily Correspondent

September 11, 2026 12:57 p.m.

If you thought this August was especially hot, you aren’t wrong. According to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, last month tied with July 2023 as the hottest month on its record, which dates back to 1940.

The global surface air temperature averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit in August. That’s almost 3 degrees above pre-industrial levels, which exceeds the 2.7-degree threshold set by the Paris Agreement, an international treaty on climate change adopted by nearly 200 nations in 2015.

“These observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans,” says Samantha Burgess, a climate scientist and deputy director of Copernicus, in the statement. “The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world.”

Western Europe had its hottest summer ever as it dealt with back-to-back heatwaves that led to at least 35,000 deaths. So did the contiguous United States, where the average temperature in August hit 75.6 degrees—3.5 degrees above the 20th-century average. It was the warmest season on the U.S.’s record, which stretches back to 1895, according to the National Centers for Environmental Information. July was even hotter, averaging 76.9 degrees and breaking the infamous Dust Bowl record set in July 1936, per Jeff Masters and Bob Henson at Yale Climate Connections.

Other parts of the world were also drier than average, including northern Mexico, parts of Canada, the Maghreb, part of the Horn of Africa, Siberia and large parts of Asia, China, South America, South Africa and northern Australia, according to Copernicus. And at 69.9 degrees, the average sea surface temperature outside the polar regions was the highest on record for any August, passing the record previously set for the month in 2023.

According to Copernicus, the record-breaking summer heat likely arose from two factors: a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific Ocean and global heating from human use of fossil fuels. Scientists note that the naturally occurring climate pattern of El Niño alone is not responsible for these temperatures.

“While El Niño is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Niño hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” says Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London, to Seth Borenstein at the Associated Press.

Quick fact: El Niño events have been growing stronger

Using records captured in corals, a study published in August found that although El Niño climate swings occur naturally, they’ve become stronger in recent decades. That’s probably happening because humans have been heating up the planet.

The Copernicus finding follows a United Nations report that warned that passing the Paris Agreement’s 2.7-degree threshold is probably unavoidable. According to the U.N. document, titled “Limiting Overshoot” and published on September 2, the world now needs to focus on minimizing peak warming and finding ways to bring temperatures back down.

Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, writes on social media that the Copernicus report is “another stark warning sign from our heating planet,” and underscores the need for humans to stop burning coal, oil and gas. “This is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling.”

Clair Barnes, an extreme weather researcher at Imperial College London, echoes that sentiment. “Until we stop burning fossil fuels, these records will continue to tumble, and the extremes will worsen faster than we are able to adapt,” she tells Matt McGrath at the BBC News. “Crucially, how much worse we allow it to get remains within our hands.”

To prevent the trawling and theft of human writing,
items.text:
Designers and Computer Scientists Create New Decoy Fonts That Humans Can Read but A.I. Bots Cannot

To prevent the trawling and theft of human writing, font-makers are employing both old and new illusions to outsmart large language models

As the deployment of A.I. tools into search engines, text messaging and writing platforms becomes increasingly conspicuous and pervasive, some researchers are seeking new ways to insulate words written by humans from the reach of trawling bots and A.I. agents.

The camouflaging technique is a modern-day version of an optical illusion known as hybrid imaging, which was made famous in 2007 when researchers at MIT created a portrait in which both Marilyn Monroe and Albert Einstein were identifiable, depending on the distance of the viewer.

Whereas those images were created to better understand human perception, Decoy Font was inspired by a desire for privacy. The font features two layers of text: one foregrounded in clear outlines and a second dark and blurred in the background. It offers human writers the chance to create cheeky juxtapositional messages, hiding the blurred “Happy Human,” for example, behind a crisp “Sorry Robot.”

MixFont’s first attempt at an anti-A.I. typeface was called Ghost Font: a slightly dizzying display that placed moving words atop a television-static-like background that also constantly shifted. The company acknowledged that it wasn’t a traditional font, because the message was readable only in a video format, but the design successfully demonstrated the limits of A.I. perception.

“I was inspired to make Ghost Font one day after texting with my mom, and I noticed that A.I. kept trying to summarize our messages, many times incorrectly,” Eric Lu, MixFont’s founder, tells Forbes’ Leslie Katz. “I was annoyed that it was being so intrusive in our private conversation, and I started brainstorming ways that I could potentially communicate without A.I. reading everything.”

Other designers have also experimented in recent months with tricking A.I. trawlers.

Fun fact: The first font

The father of the printing press, Johann Gutenberg, is largely credited with having created the first Western typeface.

His black-letter font was designed to mimic the handwritten calligraphy of monks.

In July, a collaboration of studios including Seneda & Abrucio and PlayType released ShieldFont, a typeface that scrambles text for automated scrapers. The font replaces roughly half of all “content words”—nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs—with random other words in its source code, such that the writing taken by bots is nonsensical. More than 90 percent of the resultant gibberish is rejected by quality filters, Fast Company’s Hunter Schwarz reports.

“A sentence is a sequence of decisions,” ShieldFont’s creators write in their white paper, explaining that a primary motivator for their work was to block the theft of human writing by A.I. models. “When I write, I am choosing this word rather than that one, putting this clause before that one, deciding what to leave out. The finished paragraph is a record of thinking that took effort to do. ... We are being asked to hand over the work, and to train our own replacement with it, and to do both without being told.”

ShieldFont: A Typeface that Poisons Unauthorized AI Training

MixFont “started as an exploration of how A.I. and typography intersect, but it was also meant to raise awareness of the growing reach and capabilities of A.I.,” Lu tells Dezeen’s Rima Sabina Aouf. “I think the reaction to the font shows that there are many folks who feel strong A.I. fatigue and want a way to defend themselves against the presence of A.I. in their lives.”

The massive
items.text:
Ancient Rome’s Largest Fresco and Mosaic Complex, Featuring Depictions of a Mysterious Maritime City, Opens to the Public After 2,000 Years

The massive artworks, created in the first century C.E., were discovered in the 1990s during excavations of the Baths of Trajan

Sarah Kuta
| Daily Correspondent

September 11, 2026 11:31 a.m.

For the first time in centuries, members of the public can admire what is believed to be ancient Rome’s largest fresco and mosaic complex.

This week, officials in the Italian capital unveiled the recently restored Painted City fresco and the Great Mosaic. The works were created sometime during the first century C.E. but remained hidden underground until the 1990s.

The 107-square-foot fresco depicts a walled maritime city in blue and terra cotta hues, complete with buildings, a theater, a temple, public piazzas and towers, as seen from above.

“We don’t know what city it refers to, but it must have been a particularly well-known one,” Claudio Parisi Presicce, Rome’s cultural superintendent, tells Nicole Winfield of the Associated Press (AP).

The multicolored mosaic, meanwhile, depicts decorative columns, plinths and other architectural elements, as well as additional bird’s-eye views of the unknown port city. It also features several human figures, including a bearded philosopher, a centaur, and a poet receiving a crown of laurel.

The mosaic is massive, measuring 33 feet high and 52 feet wide—and counting.

“We think it’s the biggest wall mosaic ever found in the Roman world, and we are still digging to find where it stops,” Francesco Pacetti, one of the archaeologists who excavated the finds, tells the London Times’ Tom Kington.

Archaeologists continue to reveal more of the mosaic. Right now, they’re working on a new section that depicts grape harvesting and winemaking, reports CNN’s Barbie Latza Nadeau.

The artworks were initially discovered three decades ago, during excavations of the sprawling Baths of Trajan. Designed by Apollodorus of Damascus at the request of Emperor Trajan and dedicated in 109 C.E., the Baths of Trajan spanned roughly 15 acres, forming the largest bath complex in the world at the time. Archaeologists think the complex was more than just a place to bathe; they believe it was also the setting for exercise, socializing and cultural activities.

Did you know? Roman baths

Archaeologists have discovered all kinds of artifacts in Roman baths, including teeth, scalpels, tweezers, flasks, perfume vials, animal bones, dice, coins, jewelry, needles, and fragments of plates and bowls.

The baths were built atop Oppian Hill, not far from the Colosseum, where Emperor Nero had built his lavish Domus Aurea palace between 65 and 68 C.E. The mosaic and fresco, which were discovered beneath the hill, are believed to predate the baths, so they may have once been part of the Domus Aurea, but archaeologists say their exact origins remain unclear.

The large-scale artworks will initially be open to small groups of no more than 15 people, with free guided tours available by reservation starting September 12, Ilaria Cicinelli and Tokunbo Salako report for Euronews. Authorities intend to see how the trial period goes—and how the presence of visitors affects the artworks—before they’ll consider opening the subterranean works to a wider audience. The site features rest areas, walkways, lighting and a tiered seating system for events, per Euronews.

Above ground, visitors can also now explore a large, semicircular wall known as an exedra, which archaeologists believe functioned as a library of sorts.

“The niches in the wall appear to have held books and documents,” Roberto Gualtieri, the mayor of Rome, tells the Times.

For Decades, Scientists Thought an ‘American Cheetah’ Once Roamed North America. Turns Out the Extinct Cat Wasn’t a Cheetah

Ancient DNA from fossils found in Wyoming and Canada’s Yukon Territory suggests the wild cat more closely resembled modern pumas than modern cheetahs

Sara Hashemi
| Daily Correspondent

September 11, 2026 10:00 a.m.

During the Pleistocene epoch, some 12,000 to 2.6 million years ago, a feline predator known as the American cheetah (Miracinonyx trumani) roamed the grasslands of what’s now North America. Except, according to a new study, the extinct creature wasn’t a cheetah at all.

After analyzing four fossils uncovered in Wyoming and the Yukon Territory in Canada, a team of researchers suggests that the wild cat was more closely related to the modern puma, also called the mountain lion or cougar, than to today’s cheetahs. The work, published in the journal Current Biology on September 4, offers a new understanding of the ancient animal’s range, diet and evolution.

“Calling it the American cheetah implies a specific behavior and ecology, which isn’t necessarily appropriate for this species,” says study co-author Molly Cassatt-Johnstone, a molecular ecologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, to Erin Garcia de Jesús at Science News.

The misnomer dates to when the species was first described in 1979. Scientists thought the fossils shared striking similarities with today’s cheetahs in Africa and Asia, such as elongated legs, enlarged nasal cavities and a slender build. But recent studies have complicated that assumption. In 2005, for instance, DNA evidence hinted that M. trumani evolved from a puma-like ancestor.

Evolutionarily, that makes sense, Cassatt-Johnstone tells Gizmodo’s Ellyn Lapointe. “Pumas are a new world lineage; they are found in the Americas. Cheetahs are old world, so in Asia and Africa, and so there would have had to have been a migration event if they were most closely related to cheetahs.”

Cassatt-Johnstone and colleagues made their discovery while examining the three fossils from the Yukon in northwestern Canada, reports Science News. The team initially assumed the remains belonged to pumas, since American cheetahs had never been discovered that far north.

“It wasn’t until we were able to generate the genetic data that we were able to identify them as American cheetahs,” Cassatt-Johnstone tells the outlet. “Then, that led to this whole discovery avalanche.”

Using DNA from the Yukon fossils, along with another from Wyoming, the team constructed an evolutionary tree with other wild cats. Analyses showed that M. trumani’s lineage diverged from the ancestors of modern pumas around 2.6 million years ago, while it diverged from the cheetah lineage around 4.7 million years ago. The extinct feline’s slender body—previously assumed to be a sign of its cheetah-ness—is now thought to be an example of convergent evolution. It’s a phenomenon where two unrelated or distantly related species independently evolve similar features because of similar environmental pressures.

The researchers also wanted to know what an animal with such a wide range ate, so they analyzed forms of nitrogen and carbon in all four fossils. The work hinted that the creature from Wyoming, which lived around 23,000 years ago, probably feasted on herbivores like pronghorn. On the other hand, the Yukon cats, which lived around 31,000 years ago, likely munched on fish such as salmon.

Fun fact: Flexible diet

Pumas are known as versatile predators that eat all sorts of prey: deer, horses, moose, raccoons, capybaras and even penguins. That’s probably why they’re such resilient animals, with a range that stretches from Canada to nearly the southern tip of South America.

“To find two populations of the same species with such different diets is really cool,” says Ross Barnett, an independent paleontologist who led the 2005 study but was not involved in the new work, to Tim Vernimmen at National Geographic. “That they were found in Arctic biomes is a huge finding.”

The team uncovered other climate-related specializations too. M. trumani had mutations that blocked certain genes from regulating the circadian rhythm, which suggests the animal “may have adapted to the extreme light cycles of summers and winters in northern latitudes,” Cassatt-Johnstone explains in a statement.

It was also missing a functional gene that encodes a sour taste receptor, hinting at a highly specialized diet. What’s more, all the cat species included in the study’s evolutionary tree—such as the lion and Canada lynx—shared this mutation, the team found.

“This implies it happened millions of years ago,” Cassatt-Johnstone tells National Geographic. “But it seems no one had noticed yet.”

A Genetically Modified Pig Kidney Kept a Man Alive for a Record Nine Months, Allowing Him to Wait for a Donated Human Organ

The animal organ kept Tim Andrews off dialysis for 271 days and represents the first time a pig kidney has been used as a bridge to human organ transplantation

Sarah Kuta
| Daily Correspondent

September 11, 2026 8:00 a.m.

For the first time, a genetically modified pig kidney has served as a temporary bridge to a human organ transplant, keeping a man alive and off dialysis for nine months while he waited for a human kidney to become available. Researchers describe the case in a paper published September 3 in the Lancet.

The man in question is Tim Andrews, a now 68-year-old New Hampshire resident who had been suffering from end-stage kidney disease. He was on dialysis, a process that removes excess fluid and waste from the blood when the kidneys stop working properly, and his prognosis wasn’t good.

But Andrews had heard that genetically modified pig kidneys were being tested in humans, so he decided to volunteer for the experimental—and risky—procedure.

“I didn’t think I was going to live through it, to be honest,” he tells NBC News’ David K. Li. “But I wanted to do it for humanity. I realized, ‘OK, I’m a dead man. I’m a dead man walking.’ So, I said to myself, ‘What have I done? What have I done with my life? This is an opportunity for me to do something that most people don’t get an opportunity to do, and that’s to help humanity.’”

In January 2025, surgeons at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston transplanted a kidney from a Yucatan miniature pig into Andrews. The pig, which Andrews nicknamed Wilma, had received 69 genetic edits designed to reduce the risk of porcine virus transmission and lower the chances of Andrews’ immune system rejecting the organ, reports the Guardian’s Andrew Gregory.

After recovering from the procedure, Andrews felt better than he had in years.

“I could walk around,” he tells NPR’s Rob Stein. “I wasn’t tied to a machine. I wasn’t dead tired. So, for me, it was beautiful.”

About six months after the transplant, Andrews developed a bacterial infection from methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which is resistant to many antibiotics. His doctors reduced his immunosuppression drugs, which were helping prevent his body from rejecting the foreign organ. But then the pig kidney’s blood vessels started to become damaged. Eventually, the damage escalated to organ failure.

Andrews lived with the pig kidney—and was able to avoid dialysis—for a record 271 days. Though the kidney ultimately had to be removed, doctors consider the transplant overall to be a success.

“He had a [pig] kidney that lasted nine months, which is mind-blowing,” lead author Leonardo Riella, who helped conduct Andrews’ surgeries and serves as medical director for kidney transplantation at Mass General Brigham, tells New Scientist’s Chris Simms.

After surgeons removed the pig kidney, Andrews went back on dialysis for three months. Then, in January 2026, he received a donated human kidney. These days, he spends his time swimming, riding his bike, kayaking, fishing and soaking up life.

“Every day I wake up. I’m like, [this is] another [extra] day because I should have been dead a year ago or more,” he tells NBC News, adding that he expects to live for decades.

And he remains grateful to Wilma.

“She saved my life,” he tells NPR News. “She was the bridge so that I didn’t die, so I got to the human kidney.”

Did you know? First pig kidney transplant

In March 2024, surgeons at Mass General Hospital—including Riella—transplanted a genetically modified pig kidney into a human for the first time. The patient, 62-year-old Richard Slayman, who had end-stage kidney disease, died 52 days later from seemingly unrelated cardiac issues.

Technically, the pig kidney did not completely bridge the gap for Andrews. However, “it carried the majority of the waiting time the patient had to undergo before being able to receive the human organ transplant, therefore proving the concept that it is possible,” David Mulligan, a surgeon at Yale School of Medicine who was not involved with the research, tells STAT’s Eric Boodman.

Since Andrews, Riella says his team has completed five additional pig kidney transplants. One patient, whose case will be described in a forthcoming paper, has already surpassed Andrews’ nine-month record, per New Scientist.

Taken together, the cases suggest that briefly having a pig organ in their bodies doesn’t affect how patients later react to human organ transplants.

“Right now, we don’t think there’s any downside of having a pig kidney followed by a human kidney, but when we started this, we had no idea that that would be true,” says Mike Curtis, president and CEO of eGenesis, the company developing the genetically modified pig organs used at Mass General Brigham and helping fund the research, to the New York Times’ Roni Caryn Rabin.

Some researchers consider xenotransplantation, or the use of animal organs in humans, as one possible solution to the ongoing global organ shortage. In the United States alone, nearly 110,000 individuals are on the national transplant waiting list.

Kidneys are a particularly urgent target because chronic kidney disease often requires patients to undergo dialysis, a costly and time-consuming treatment that can dramatically disrupt daily life. More than 95,000 individuals in the U.S. are waiting for a kidney transplant, yet in 2025, fewer than 28,000 patients received a human kidney. Around 12 people die each day waiting for a donated kidney.

“The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” Riella says in a statement. “We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.”

Doctors say we’re still likely years away from pig kidneys eliminating the need for human kidney transplants. But in the meantime, animal organs could serve as a stopgap for patients waiting for a human one.

“Maybe the first more reachable goal is for this treatment to be a bridge, and maybe 10 or 15 years from now, we may be talking about an alternative as good as human kidneys,” Riella tells the Times. “We’re at the beginning of the journey.”

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.
An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.
An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died
Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.
Fall restaurant season is HERE
Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.
An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address
Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.
Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.
Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.
A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.
A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.
September 4
A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn
Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.
Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.
The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.
Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.
Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.
A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.
What’s happening with Food?
Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.
A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.
An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.
